analysis.investment_thesis: IFCI is a government-owned NBFC that has spent the better part of a decade destroying capital — revenue has fallen at -9.2% CAGR over nine years, net losses totalled thousands of crores across FY17-FY22, and FCF was negative INR 1,011 Cr in FY25 alone. Trading at 41x trailing earnings with ROE of 2.6%, this is an expensive ticket to a business going nowhere.
key_strengths: Government ownership provides an implicit sovereign guarantee, preventing outright failure and allowing continued borrowing access
Recent profitability (INR 349 Cr in FY25) and sharply reduced debt (INR 3,714 Cr vs INR 7,162 Cr in FY22) show some deleveraging progress
Large legacy asset base (total assets INR 23,540 Cr) with potential resolution value from NPA recoveries
key_risks: Revenue has shrunk from INR 4,465 Cr (FY16) to INR 1,879 Cr (FY25) — this is a franchise in secular decline, not a recovery story
ROE of only 2.6% means the business earns less than the cost of equity; shareholders would be better served by liquidation at book value
FCF was negative INR 1,011 Cr in FY25 and positive in only 1 of the last 5 years — the company consumes more cash than it generates
red_flags: Negative P/S ratio (-27.86x) is a data anomaly flagging deeply abnormal revenue accounting — not a business I can evaluate with confidence
Operating Margin reported at 117.9% is mathematically nonsensical for a lending institution and signals accounting complexity or data distortion
41x P/E on INR 349 Cr of profit for an institution with a nine-year history of losses is speculative, not value — the market is buying a government restructuring option, not a business
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Charlie Munger and I have a simple rule: if you have to work very hard to understand why a business is good, it probably is not. IFCI fails at the first test — the reported operating margin of 117.9% and a negative P/S ratio signal financial statement irregularities or structural accounting that I cannot reconcile. Even setting that aside, the underlying business is unambiguously in decline: revenues have fallen by more than half over nine years, and the accumulated losses from FY17-FY22 wiped out a substantial portion of the equity base.

The recent return to profitability is real — INR 241 Cr in FY24 and INR 349 Cr in FY25 — and is primarily driven by reduced finance costs (down 84% since FY16) and NPA resolutions rather than franchise growth. But paying 41x earnings for a company with ROE of 2.6%, negative FCF, and a shrinking loan book is not value investing — it is speculation on a government restructuring that may never fully materialise. I have no interest in government-sponsored financial institutions with poor return track records at premium valuations.
